title: Controlling the Inhomogeneous Broadening and Impedance Matching of a Spin Ensemble
authors: Mathieu Couillard, Debdip Guchait, Hiroki Takahashi, Yuimaru Kubo
abstract: We control the spectral distribution of a spin ensemble by applying a magnetic field gradient using an anti-Helmholtz coil inside a dilution refrigerator, and demonstrate impedance matching between the ensemble and a transmission line, achieving -50 dB absorption of incident radiation. This represents a first step toward a spin-ensemble-based quantum memory for itinerant microwave photons. We further model the spectral distribution under the applied gradient to predict the spin-resonator response, and use the device to systematically tune the weak-to-strong coupling transition in both continuous-wave and time-domain pulsed measurements.
summary: The research demonstrates a novel method to control the spectral properties of a spin ensemble by applying an external magnetic field gradient. By achieving impedance matching and tuning the inhomogeneous broadening in situ, the authors show a crucial step toward realizing robust, controllable quantum memories for microwave photons.
main_problem: The primary goal is to control the spectral distribution (inhomogeneous broadening) of a spin ensemble while simultaneously achieving impedance matching with microwave photons.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated tunable, in situ control over inhomogeneous broadening using a magnetic field gradient and achieved near-perfect absorption by tuning the system to impedance matching ($C=1$).
method:
They used an anti-Helmholtz coil setup within a dilution refrigerator to apply controlled magnetic field gradients ($
abla B$) to tune the spin ensemble's spectral properties, measured via microwave spectroscopy (VNA).
model_or_system: The system involves a spin ensemble (DPPH molecules) coupled to a high-quality factor dielectric resonator. The physics is modeled using concepts from cavity QED, treating the coupling strength and linewidth ($\Gamma$) as key parameters.
key_observables: Reflection spectrum ($|S_{11}|^2$), spectral distribution $ho(\omega)$, Rabi oscillations (in time domain), and absorption efficiency.
important_parameters:
Inhomogeneous linewidth ($\Gamma$), Cooperativity ($C$), magnetic field gradient ($
abla B$), and coupling strength ($g_{ens}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling the spectral distribution as a convolution of initial broadening with gradient-induced broadening, and fitting data to specific functional forms like semi-ellipses.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the magnetic field cross-section generated by the anti-Helmholtz coil, the dielectric resonator setup, and show spectroscopic measurements demonstrating the collapse of Rabi oscillations as the gradient increases.
paper_structure:
The paper progresses from establishing the physical platform (dielectric resonator + spin ensemble) to detailing the control mechanism ($
abla B$ application), presenting spectral characterization results (impedance matching), and finally showing time-domain dynamics (Rabi oscillation quenching).
why_interesting: This work directly addresses fundamental challenges in quantum memory: controlling decoherence sources ($\Gamma$) externally while optimizing coupling ($C=1$) for efficient photon storage/retrieval, which is central to building quantum networks.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. a) Cross section of the simulated static magnetic field z- component, produced by the anti-Helmholtz coils with the coil axis along the z-direction. The 4 black rectangles represent cross sections of the coils, the lines are contour lines of constant Bz, and the sample is contained in the white box outlined at the center of the plot. The simulation has 9000 Turns per coil and driven with a current of 200 mA. b) Close up of the sample region, where the field is shown to be well approximated as linear along the z-direction.

FIG. 2. (a) Anti-Helmholtz coils integrated into the tail of the still shield, inside which the dielectric resonator is housed. (b) The entire still shield tail and the device, which sit inside the superconducting vector magnet (not shown here, see the supplementary material). (c) Simulated ac magnetic-field amplitude of the resonator’s fundamen- tal mode. The direction of the ac field is indicated by the black ar- rowed circles, and the static magnetic field by Bz. The rutile crystal has an outer diameter of 8 mm, an inner diameter of 1 mm, and a height of 2 mm.

FIG. 4. Reflection spectrum as a function of probe frequency and magnetic field when a magnetic field gradient is applied such that C = 1. a) is the experimental data and b) is the fitted spectrum us- ing the fitted parameters from a). The white dashed lines are the resonance frequencies of the polaritons and the spectra on the right correspond to black vertical lines, where the spins are in resonance with the resonator.

FIG. 3. Reflection spectrum as a function of probe frequency and magnetic field when no magnetic field gradient was applied, corre- sponding to the high cooperativity regime. a) is the experimental data and b) is the fitted spectrum using the fitted parameters from a). The white dashed lines are the resonance frequencies of the polaritons and the spectra on the right correspond to black vertical lines, where the spins are on resonance with the resonator.

FIG. 5. Spin spectral distribution data(light) and fit(dark) for various magnetic field gradients. The legend lists ∆B, the magnetic field dif- ference on either side of the sample. The zero current data is fit to a Lorentzian function, while all the others are fit to semi-ellipses using only the data in the central region.

Spintronics.note: The demonstration of achieving near-perfect absorption by tuning the system to impedance matching ($C=1$) in a spin ensemble coupled to a resonator directly relates to cavity QED concepts central to spintronics.
